title: A house open wide (Avot 1:5)
hook: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household

segments.voice: Yesterday, mitabek: sit in the dust of the wise. This first week of camp five opened Pirkei Avot: the chain handed down, judge slowly, three legs to stand on, and not for the prize. Today, the other Yose talks about your front door. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

Some homes you just walk into. The door's unlocked, there's always something on the stove, and nobody asks why you came. Kids from down the street end up at dinner. A cousin sleeps on the couch for a month. Other homes, lovely ones, are closed: you visit by appointment, and you leave before it gets awkward. Plenty are somewhere in between. The first Yose opened his house to the wise. His partner, Yose from Jerusalem, goes further. Not just the wise. Everyone.
screen: `THE HOUSE YOU JUST WALK INTO.` → `VISITS BY APPOINTMENT.` → `NOT JUST THE WISE.`

segments.voice: Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem says, in paraphrase: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household. In Hebrew, open wide is patuach lirvacha. Revach means space, room, relief: a house where someone in trouble can breathe. The rabbis pictured Abraham's tent. A midrash says it had openings on all four sides, so a traveler coming from any direction would find a door facing them. In Genesis, Abraham runs out in the heat of the day to greet three strangers. That's the model. Then the second half: let the poor be members of your household. Not guests at the back door. Not a donation in an envelope. Family. At the table, in the conversation, known by name. Some commentators note the dignity in it: a poor person treated like a member of the house doesn't have to feel ashamed to be there. Honesty requires one more note. The same saying continues with a warning against too much idle talk with women, words that some readers today find troubling, and that commentators over the centuries have explained, limited and argued about. I won't pretend it isn't there. But the first line is the one to carry today: an extra chair at Shabbat dinner, a stranger at the seder, a door that opens easily.
screen: `PATUACH LIRVACHA — OPEN WIDE.` · `ABRAHAM'S TENT, FOUR DOORS.` · `THE POOR AS FAMILY.` · `A HARDER LINE, HONESTLY NAMED.` · then, large: `OPEN THE DOOR WIDE.`

segments.voice: Picture your front door, and who hasn't come through it in a long time, or ever: a neighbor who lives alone, a new coworker far from home, someone in a hard stretch, a student with nowhere to go on a holiday. Picture them at your table. Then choose one simple invitation you could offer: coffee, a walk, a plate of leftovers.
Patuach lirvacha. Open to spaciousness: Yose ben Yochanan's saying that a house should open wide, with the poor as members of the household.
Your line: open the door wide. Wide enough that anyone, from any direction, finds a way in. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 238 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A TEACHER AND A FRIEND.`

howItsDone: Hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests, is a Jewish practice: guests are invited to Shabbat and holiday meals, and early in the seder the Haggadah invites all who are hungry to come and eat.

trapdoor: what it means: a home open in every direction, where people in need are treated as family.
what a scholar hears: Avot de-Rabbi Natan pictures a house open on all sides like Abraham's tent, and the Mishnah itself goes on to a line about women that later sages limited and debated.

an open book, a life with nothing kept hidden
open-handed, giving freely to charity outside

Inviting only scholars and wise people to your table.
Giving the poor money at the door, so they needn't come in.

notes: The second half of 1:5 (on not talking much with women) is named honestly but not taught; a Keeper should confirm the framing is fair to both traditional and modern readers.

Reference to Abraham greeting three strangers assumes earlier camp-4 days covered Genesis 18 (Vayera); confirm.
